Fleeting Gold

Fall in the Colorado foothills is a lot like a good sunset: spectacular, and gone before you're ready for it. So on a Sunday in early October I drove up to Evergreen, a mountain town west of Denver at a little over 7,000 feet, to catch it while I could. I started on a rocky perch above the trees, where a granite dome pokes out of the pine and fir and the far ridges turn blue with distance.

Then I wandered into the aspens, which is a little ironic in a town called Evergreen. Their chalk-white trunks climbed toward a clean blue sky, and the leaves overhead ran from lime to lemon. Along the road a few groves had already hit full yellow, while the one I walked through was still halfway there. That yellow isn't new. It was in the leaves all summer, hidden under the green, and it only shows once the trees stop making chlorophyll. The leaves are thin enough that low sun shines right through them, so for photos, put the sun behind the grove and shoot toward it.

By late afternoon the light had turned honey-colored. Long shadows crept across a meadow of straw-gold grass, and on the far side of it stood what looked like a timber barn with a red metal roof, so of course I stopped. Then, as the light faded, I found a herd of elk grazing beside a creek in town, right up against the road, like they owned the place! It was still rut season, when bulls get testy, so keep your distance; I shot from the car window. The gold only lasts a week or two, and for one Sunday I got to stand in it.
